name: Andromeda XV
quote: Two new relatively luminous (MV ∼ −9) dwarf galaxies And XV and XVI are found in the study // However, we discuss briefly here two new dwarf galaxies which were discovered immediately from simple visual inspection of the starcounts maps.
reader_note: Label used without an argument for galaxy vs cluster. RGB, distance, profile and MV are measured but not offered as grounds; 'relatively luminous' is descriptive. A reader could arguably code L; flagged for adjudication.

name: Andromeda XV
quote: And XV (discovered by Ibata et al. 2007), is a reasonably bright (MV = −9.8, LV = 7.1 × 105 L ), relatively isolated dSph
reader_note: dSph label taken as given. The paper's kinematic confirmation statement names only And XVIII, XXI and XXII; And XV is noted as an outlier in mass-size-luminosity relations, attributed to possible tidal stripping.

name: Andromeda XVIII
quote: Given these current data, all of the CMDs appear to show stellar populations typical of dSph galaxies. // Andromeda XVIII appears to possess stellar populations typical of dSph galaxies.
location: Sec. 2 (Discovery and stellar populations); Sec. 4 (Andromeda XVIII, position and morphology)
reader_note: Only stated ground is a CMD resemblance (clear RGB, few or no young main-sequence/blue-loop stars) to dSph populations, not an age spread. Borderline P vs N; flagged for adjudication.

name: Andromeda XVIII
quote: Andromeda XVIII is an isolated dwarf galaxy 579 kpc away from the nearest large galaxy, M31.
reader_note: Kind taken as given. The paper discusses extended star formation (citing Makarova et al. 2017: 'comparatively continuous star formation for several Gyr prior to ceasing 1.5 Gyr ago') and old plus intermediate populations, but not as grounds for the kind; a reader could code P. Note: Tollerud et al. 2012 (arXiv:1112.1067), read for And XV, reports the first spectroscopy of And XVIII and states 'these observations [...] definitively confirm it as a kinematically cold satellite galaxy' (D), i.e. an earlier kinematic paper than the listed vlos reference.

name: Andromeda XX
quote: These galaxies - christened Andromeda XVIII, XIX and XX after the constellation in which they are found - have stellar populations which appear typical of dSph galaxies. // Given these current data, all of the CMDs appear to show stellar populations typical of dSph galaxies.
reader_note: Same population ground as And XVIII (CMD resemblance, not an age spread); And XX's RGB is described as 'poorly populated'. It was first noticed by eye 'during a search for globular clusters', but no cluster label is given. Borderline P vs N; flagged.

name: Andromeda XX
quote: And XX was the third of three dSphs discovered by McConnachie et al. (2008), and is notable for being one of the faintest dSph companions detected surrounding Andromeda thus far.
reader_note: dSph label taken as given; 4 candidate members.

name: Andromeda XXIV
quote: These two galaxies resemble the traditional dSphs belonging to the MW group in many ways. // They have small halflight-radii (rh = 357 pc and 232 pc) and are relatively faint (MV = −7.6±0.5 and −7.1±0.5). // the three with MV > −9 (And XXIV, And XXVI and And XXVII) have half-light radii typical of both M31 and MW dSphs in this magnitude range.
location: Sec. 5 (Discussion, And XXIV and And XXVI); Sec. 4 (size-luminosity relation)
reader_note: Also states And XXIV 'is perhaps the galaxy with the clearest sign of having a simple stellar population' (narrow metallicity spread); not a cluster label, recorded for completeness.

name: Andromeda XXIV
quote: Given the lower quality of this dataset in comparison to the remainder of those we present in this work, and the overlap of And XXIV in velocity space with contamination from the MW, a robust kinematic detection and characterisation of this galaxy is made incredibly challenging. // As such, we present these results as a tentative identification of And XXIV, and do not include its measured properties in the remainder of our analysis.
reader_note: Galaxy/dSph label taken as given. The 'tentative identification' concerns the kinematic detection (3 probable members), not the kind; not coded X. Flagged in case the adjudicator reads it otherwise.

name: Bootes I
quote: With a characteristic scale length of 220 pc, the size of the object is typical of the Galactic dwarf spheroidal satellites. // Even though the CMD resembles that of a globular cluster, this is emphatically not the case for the object’s morphology and size. // If, as seems likely, it is a dwarf galaxy, then Boo is one of the faintest (MV ∼ −5.m 8) so far discovered.
reader_note: Hedged ('possibly a dwarf galaxy', 'as seems likely') but the authors argue explicitly against a disrupted globular cluster on size, orbit and mass-segregation grounds. Coded L, not X.

name: Bootes I
quote: which confirm Boo I as a dark matterdominated ([value]; [value]), metal-poor ([Fe/H] = −2.3; σ[Fe/H] = 0.3) galaxy (Jenkins et al. 2021).
reader_note: Restates earlier literature (Jenkins et al. 2021 and others). The UFD label is otherwise used throughout without further argument. This 2025/2026 paper is clearly not the first published dispersion for Bootes I; the earlier original was not read here.

name: Bootes II
quote: With a physical half-light size that is an order of mag larger than most GCs but similar to those of dSphs, we are inclined to designate Boötes II a dwarf galaxy. // While follow-up observations will reveal the candidate’s true nature in more detail, its size and luminosity are consistent with those of the other recent detections that have been labeled dwarfs spheroidals.
reader_note: Hedged: the abstract places it 'in an apparent 40 < rh < 100 pc void between globular clusters and dwarf galaxies'. The authors still adopt the galaxy designation, so coded L, not X. Borderline; flagged for adjudication.

name: Eridanus IV
quote: The position of Eri IV in this space is consistent with the known population of ultra-faint dwarf galaxies, suggesting a dwarf galaxy classification for the system. // In particular, the large physical size [...] and ellipticity [...] of Eri IV are inconsistent with the population of comparably bright globular clusters // Based on the high likelihood that this system is a dwarf galaxy, rather than a star cluster, we adopt the dwarf galaxy naming convention
reader_note: The title calls it a 'Candidate' and the paper says spectroscopy 'could provide evidence'. The authors adopt the galaxy label on morphology, so coded L, not X. Orbital properties are also mentioned as weaker support.

name: Eridanus IV
quote: Eri IV and Cen I both exhibit high mass-to-light ratios typical of dwarf galaxies at similar magnitudes, which are much greater than the mass-to-light ratio of [value] characteristic of MW globular clusters // We therefore conclude that both Eri IV and Cen I are dark matterdominated dwarf galaxies. // When compared to other dwarf galaxies and globular clusters, the morphological and orbital parameters of Eri IV are consistent with those of the dwarf galaxies.
reader_note: Main ground is D. L appears as a supporting comparison and in 'identified as dwarf galaxy candidates based on their physical size'. A metallicity dispersion is measured but not offered as a ground.

name: Grus I

name: Grus I
quote: Under the assumption of dynamical equilibrium, our analysis confirms that Grus I is a dark-matter-dominated UFD ([value]). // In this regard, Grus I is a particularly interesting Milky Way satellite as its classification has remained somewhat ambiguous.
reader_note: Describes the earlier classification as 'somewhat ambiguous' (citing Walker et al. 2016 and photometric studies), then resolves it by dynamics; not coded X because the paper itself concludes. The metallicity dispersion is not resolved (upper limit only). Low mean metallicity and neutron-capture deficiency (citing Ji et al. 2019) are mentioned as hints, but these fit no code. Not the first vlos paper: Walker et al. 2016 and Zoutendijk et al. 2021 are cited as earlier.
